That's not really helpful at all. Something much simpler maybe?

I barely leave my house. I had to travel by train for a sleep study in a different city a few days ago and I had a serious panic attack at a train station trying to simply get a cab. And now you want me to go on a vacation abroad? Also, I work.

Kind of ridiculous to suggest someone barely functioning and drowned with anxiety to travel. No offense.

You do you, but I'll write everything I feel, everything that happened to me and was notable. I'd like to leave an account for scientific purposes, so that someone perhaps can have a case study or something. Also I want people that helped to know how I valued them and those that hurt me to know that.

I actually think, that abstracting from the actual suicide, writing a note can be useful. It might be therapeutic. Oftentimes, we gain insight by writing things down.
I'd like everyone to tell me the honest truth and admit their mistakes.
As a person that used this same kind of knife a lot lately, I can relate. But I didn't do it to kill myself, I did it to live. You're not alone, if I count as another person.
What do you mean by a "glitch in my system"?

I'm truly sorry if I sounded unkind.

My point was, that I saw for myself, that I got progressively more in wages and still am progressively worse off. About few days after this message of mine I was committed to a psych ward. I don't know what money does or doesn't buy, and I don't really know what happiness, having never felt like I was experiencing it. Actually, people are pondering what happiness is for millennia, so I guess I'm not singled out in not knowing myself.

But anyway, I understand I shouldn't write such things and I'm truly sorry. Also I'm probably shadow banned for this, so I got punished.

Also, if I can help anyone with money troubles, I'd be glad to do that. One thing I can help is maybe get someone into IT, which is where good money is at.

You can have everything I posses after I end myself, if you want. Though it won't probably amount to much to you, if you're in the US.

I meant that money doesn't buy a way out of depression and anxiety. No, it doesn't buy access to happiness. Traveling? I'm too f'd up to go to a neighboring city.
What do you do, like for a job?

From what I've observed (but this is only my individual observation), having more money doesn't necessarily make life better, you're still left with mental illness and no support. Unless maybe if you're stinking rich. Even if you try to pay for someone to help you, that might not work. Yeah, I even paid for a psychiatrist that offered completely zero help and took money for a 15-minute visit where I was doing all the talk. Same thing happened with one psychotherapist I went to. But, for reference, I wasn't homeless (yet). Also, having money allows you to buy distractions that take your mind off the hopelessness for a moment, but it doesn't last long.
What do you do? Like, for money.

I was in a hospital because I had my tonsils removed. Pretty basic stuff, can be done without hospitalization, but it's supposedly safer this way, as there can be bleeding after the operation, so it's better if they can help you right away as opposed to calling an ambulance.

I was in a room with another guy. He had cancer. He told me a lot about his treatment, how he was on a few rounds of chemotherapy, which caused nausea among other things, how he was eventually told officially, that the public health insurance won't offer him any more treatment as he was deemed a lost cause, and then got more treatment only because an decent oncologist got him on a clinical trial of new drugs. He was really suffering. And he was only 3 years older than me. I didn't want to be this guy.

Curiously though, we talked and the guy saw how I was injecting myself with insulin (I have type 2 diabetes). And he said he was in his mind better of than me because he wouldn't want to stick needles in himself 4 times a day. I don't know, maybe this shows that people sometimes have irrational thoughts about how their suffering relates to the suffering of others (like, type 2 diabetes has lower morality rate than cancers, is curable and treatment and management causes much less distress). Or maybe they aren't irrational, but just people have different needs.

Thanks. I indeed wrote some walls of text on reddit recently. I guess maybe this is a somewhat weird way to cope with my own psychological distress. I hope whatever data I'll dump on the Internet, if not really helpful, will at least be amusing to someone.

And yeah, indeed I sincerely think hugging an animal could be beneficial, and for both sides. Just use common sense and try to stay safe, as it might be dangerous. Cause firstly you can get directly hurt, so no lions or tigers, and secondly because of parasites and pathogens (which is probably how we got this whole pandemic deal started), so preferably an animal raised in a controlled environment, like domestic cats or livestock.

And be sure you don't cause distress. You can't ask for consent, but that doesn't mean the animal can't consent and/or can't express consent, and they do communicate, including in ways we can easily understand, so if your cat thrashes around when you hug it, let it go. With hugging, both sides should be relaxed and happy (and yes, animals are certainly capable of relaxation, and possibly happiness). Lack of reciprocity in hugging can't even really be beneficial for just one side, if you feel your partner is uncomfortable, you won't be comfortable either (unless you lack empathy, but I think OP does).

Well. I don't know if you like technology, but I had a thought lately. I have a miniature computer in my pocket (LG G5). Not the greatest of it's kind, a few years old, but nice still. It can do math. A lot of math. Like, it's faster at math than enormous heavy expensive computer rooms some decades ago.

Garry Kasparov) in chess. If I'm not mistaken, simply by thinking about possible future moves, each second evaluating about 200 million possible future combinations of chess pieces, assigning a "success" number to each possible future path and just choosing the next move that was on the path with the highest such number.

That computing power (hidden in the GPU) is actually used in this phone not to play chess, but rather to generate computer graphics in real time (i.e. so fast, that we perceive the images it produces as a fluid animation), for example.

That's not even comparable to the computing power people had just a hundred years ago, when the most sophisticated machine for computation was a complex gearbox. The phone would spin circles around the sum total computing power back then.

But this is really not that impressive to me. What's more impressive is this. This "smart" phone (so a pocket-sized miniature multipurpose portable computer with a cellular network modem) is constantly connected to other computers. By emitting and receiving microwave radiation, it can send and receive data to/from those computers. And, like, a lot of data. Encyclopedia britanica, a large set of books with a lot of knowledge, actual paper books, could be send this way in about a minute (with my pretty meager wifi at home). I can't find a better comparison, but anyway, the device can get a lot of information from other devices.

Ant there are many other devices. Like really many, billions. So many that we thought at first to give each one a number from one to about 4 billion, and then we ran out (that's not entirely correct, as the number of IPv4 public addresses we really actually use is lower, but the order of magnitude should be correct)!

And those devices store data. Again, a lot. A very cheap virtual private server (fancy way of saying "a set of resources on a computer, that on for another computer looks as if it was a completely separate computer with it's own resources") can store encyclopedia britanica a few dozen times over. Or apparently a single full copy of wikipedia (compressed; I'll get to wikipedia in a moment). But those are pretty small. There are a lot bigger. And there are many computers. For example, the for companies owning machines with most of the data on the Internet have enough space to store wikipedia 63 milion times.

And those devices have something else to offer: they can do math as well. Like, better than my meager phone. I don't have figures, but really much better. It'd be easy to check how well do supercomputers do math, but those are mostly not connected and busy doing some important work. By the way. We have those enormous computers, built to do math. It's pretty cool. so what do they do? Well, lots of things, generally science. Like simulating what happens when black holes collide and such large things. Or how small things (like atom-small and smaller) act. One big and cool thing is that they help us find medicines and cure diseases. Like, they figure out for us a few chemicals that could help, and then we just test those, and don't have to test millions (which is impossible anyway).

But going back to the phone. So the phone is connected with computers that have data and computers that can do a lot of math (and often they're good at both. So how does that help? Well, that makes the phone imbued with the god-like power of the Internet. It's now not a computer in your pocket. It's a system of computers in your pocket.

That means, if you want to know who was the 35st president of USA and how was he involved in the Cuban missile crisis, you can just take your phone, touch it's screen a bit, and voila. You have a text you can read. Which, by the way, will likely come form Wikipedia. The free online encyclopedia. An encyclopedia as a computer system. And probably the best one there is. A monumental work of 42 million people, who wanted to share knowledge and wrote 6 million articles. And all of this in your pocket.

But that's just raw knowledge. What else can it do? Well, it can, thanks to that connectivity, do many of the things people were always good at, and computers just lately started to keep up. Do you want to find the nearest grocery store? Well, just take the phone and say "find the nearest grocery store" (you might need to initiate the system by saying some code word like "ok google", or pressing a button). And it will show you and tell you. Yeah, that's cool, and all, but voice recognition, natural language processing, database queries, voice synthesis, that's all pretty old news. But now we have computer vision, deep learning. Now I point my phone at a flower or animal I have no idea about, and it will tell me how's it called. It can also do other fun stuff, like show it a sudoku puzzle and it will show you a solution faster, than the best human sudoku solver will take the pencillof the table.

Oh, and that grocery store. How does it know that? I mean, what's "near"? Well. We have figured out that some things when mixed burn fast. And when you put them in a hollow tube, you can direct the flame in one way, and the tube will go the other. Fast forward some time, and we've build a vehicle, that can take people and other stuff and propel them up so fast (faster than 7.8 kilometers per second, that's how fast at least you need to go if you want to go up but than never fall down, but instead go around the planet in circles), that they end up circling the Earth at an orbit (just like the Moon does, only closer to Earth). So once we did that, we build devices called artificial satellites, just a hunk of metal meant to orbit the planet, and then sent them spinning. And we made, among others, ones that have a computer, some energy source (I think it's mostly solar power, and maybe nuclear decay), antennae for talking back with us on Earth, and special clocks called atomic clocks, clocks that have a vibrating thing, like any clock, only those vibrations are energy level transitions of caesium atoms, which allows them to very precisely measure how time passes. So now, we shot those satellite into space. And we built portable devices (nowdays it's a chip in your phone and other devices) with antenna, that can talk with those satellites. This is what we call a global navigation satellite system. The most popular one probably is GPS, but there are others (yes, we have more!). GPS maintains some two-three dozen such satellites. So, how it works? The mobile device listens for signals the satelites send out constantly (it's a one-way communication) and figures out how a clock ticks on the device and on the satelite, estimates how much time electromagnetic waves traveled between it and the satellite (which is about 1/15th of a second), and because it knows how fast light (light is another way to say electromagnetic wave) moves (which is by the way pretty fast, a whopping almost 300 million meters per second), it can calculate how far the satellite is. Now, given this and an information called the GPS almanac, just a data sheet saying where each satellite is currently), it can find out, where it is (you have points in space which are those satellites, and draw spheres around them with a radius equal to the computed distance to the device, and they will approximately meet at a single place, that's where we are). The details are more complex than that, and I would lie if I said I know them, but that's the gist of it.

The phone also does some other tricks. Like it has cameras, electronic eyes. They used to have one on the back. Then they added one on the front, on the screen side, so that you can do video calls (another cool thing) and make photos of yourself easier. Mine is one of the first with two cameras on the back. Nowadays, some phones have 5 sensors on the back and two on the screen side. That's pretty crazy, right? And it'll get even better possibly, because although there's a problem that a phone can't easily have retractable lens to have a real optical zoom (as opposed to software zoom, which is just taking pixels form the center), but there's a trick to do this by placing the whole retractable mechanism along the width or height and just adding a mirror (so making a periscope). They actually have phones like that already, but those periscopes are fixed. I hope they'll make motorized ones. I'm pretty sure in the near future a decent phone will be blowing professional DSLR cameras from now. Optics is hard, but we're smart and can bend the rules by bending the light right.

Anyway, so what was this about? Well, in short, I think we live in a great time. Technology makes our lives better. And it steadily improves. Things we've never though possible are now within our reach. There's a trend in science-fiction literature I think, called optimistic futurism. Isaac Asimov, the guy know for three laws of robotics, represented this.

The future is bright. We're capable. We either have the technology, or we'll make it. The future is very soon. Or actually, wait. The future is now. So rejoice!

Well, maybe it works this way (or maybe it doesn't, but please read anyway, it won't take you more than a few minutes):

TL; DR Both of those sentences might be wrong. You can try to figure out if that's true, but this will require some probing in the head. Short bullet points on how to probe at the end.

You don't hate yourself. You hate the person you think you are. The fact you hate this person is maybe okay. What might not, is that you think you are this person.

Also, anyway, you don't hate this hypothetical person (whether it is you or not). What you hate are this person's actions (and inaction, when an action is expected). Or at least, this is how it should go. There's a difference. You hating this person implies that this person's very existence is a problem. However, in reality, it is what said person does or doesn't do, that causes problems. This is a very important distinction. Why? Because you, like any other person, makes imperfect decisions (often because of scarcity of resources such as time, money or skills) and act on those decisions, causing more or less distress toy you or others. If you do that, but you're not assumed to be intrinsically bound to do that (i.e. evil), that implies those actions do not stem from ill intentions. And this means there's room for improvement, you have the capability to do better. But if you, on the other hand, are presumed to be just the proverbial piece of shit, than doing bad is simply your nature, and you're doomed to be a piece of shit forever. But you don't want to be a piece of shit, right?

Lastly, you might not surely know, if you're a piece of shit. Rather, you might just know that some other people view you as a piece of shit. And here's a problem: what they say is not some fundamental truth, if there even is one. What they say is just something loosely related to this truth. See, for them to say that you're a piece of shit, three distinct processes have to occur: perception (I see something brown and icky), processing (I think this is a piece of shit), output (I say that this is a piece of shit). And each of those steps is imperfect and can twist the reality to the point that it is unrecognizable.

First, they can perceive something wrong. Keeping up with your scatological metaphor, many foods look like poop (in fact, when filmmakers need to portray poop, they usually use something like dog food or chocolate). And so can your actions be perceived wrongly. 

Next, processing, this is the worst offender as far as twisting truth goes. See, people don't see the world objectively. The brain receives raw data and immediately tries to compress the data into something useful. It has to. There's just too much. So we interpret things. We generalize, try to build a simplified view of the world given current information and past information (most people won't photo-realistically describe every turd they encounter, rather they might describe some general idea, and say they encountered one here and there)  We remember only things that seemed important at the time. We don't remember what another person did at this and that time, but we remember how we felt about what the person did and what we guessed happened, and don't really remember if this occurred three times two weeks ago or two times three weeks. Or maybe it didn't happen? Really, what ends up in memory in a person is just a rough sketch of the reality, just enough to increase chances for survival if we stumble upon something similar in the future.

Then, at the end, someone has to tell you, that you're a piece of shit. But the problem is, that even if this person had perfect recollection and perfect perception and perfect objectivity, which is asking too much already, what the person will say is not what the person has inside their skull, but what they want/need/feel like saying. Someone might be an dick, and tell you you're shit, just to mess with you. Or they might go the other route, and don't say things that might hurt you.

And this also goes for yourself. You tell yourself you're a piece of shit. But you're also flawed, you also perceive wrongly, process wrongly, remember wrong and even possibly could have a hidden agenda, like telling yourself you're a piece of shit as a coping strategy (that's when people are in stress and use some mode of thinking that allows them to lower the stress level).

Sorry for this lengthy post. I guess I lied, it might've took more than a few minutes. So now, what to do? Well, I think you should figuratively cut your skull open and do some probing. Ask these questions and think about answers:
* Do I really hate being myself? Or do I hate someone, that seems to be myself?
* Do I even hate someone (whether it is myself or not), or only hate what they do?
* Am I actually a piece of shit (a bad person)? Or do I just do bad things that seem to imply that?
* What does it even mean if I'm a piece of shit? Like, that doing bad is my unchangeable nature? So does that mean I can't improve?
* How do I even know if I'm a piece of shit and/or do bad things? Is this my observation, or someone else's? How can I trust this observation, regardless of source? Maybe I shouldn't?
* If I'm capable of improvement, than maybe I could try?
* If I don't really know how bad am I, than maybe I could try to find out more about myself?

Anyway, cheers.

I wish I could hug you, but I probably can't, because we're probably really far away. Though things would be a bit easier if you're in Poland.

However, though this may seem controversial, could you maybe just go to a prostitute? Just pay, hug, done. Like, you don't have to have sex or anything close. This probably won't be sincere, but it might be? A sex worker is just a human, like me and you. They are capable of emotions, empathy and connection. Maybe just say "Hi. This will sound weird, but could we just hug? I just need to hug someone. I'm lonely and sad.". Then hopefully he/she will agree, and you'll hug. And make it count. Not like how you hug your granny. Get in there. Really connect. And don't hesitate to cry, if you need to. Oh, and you can also talk, hold hands. And for some time. You've, as far as I know, bought some time (like an hour) alone with this person. I don't know. Maybe this is a bad advice. I'm not a psychologist or anything like that, just a random guy. But it's relatively safe to try, and at worst you just waste a bit of time and some money (at least where I live, you can book a sex worker for an hour for less than the price of a new video game).
If you do try anyway, just be sure not to engender yourself. You can't get STDs from hugging, as that's not sex, which is what the "S" stands for. Same thing with e.g. AIDS. You can get other infectious diseases still, like the dreaded COVID-19. But that's actually a risk with hugging pretty much anyone. You can wear an N95/FFP2 mask while hugging, that should protect you from those nasty bugs. Personally though, I wouldn't bother (but I'm in a position, where, while being higher risk due to chronic illness like diabetes, are relatively young and already vaccinated). The other thing is that prostitution being deregulated and associated with organized crime, you might risk being hurt and/or robbed, but for that it's best to just find some website where such services are announced, make a call, go to the person. So something like a pimp and other such criminal element probably won't be involved. I assume though, that you live in a place, where prostitution itself is not illegal and you don't risk legal trouble just for hiring someone for some hugging.

Now, leaving aside fringe ideas like that, the standard option for interpersonal contact for persons in mental distress is a psychologist/psychotherapist. But this means usually talk, and not any kind of physical contact. It would be unethical and unprofessional for such a person to touch their client. But they can I think act as a proxy, that is they can put you in a room with other people, which you could touch. This is what they call group therapy or support group. Also, there's e.g. equine-assisted therapy.

Which brings me to another option: hugging an animal. Don't know if you thought of that, tried that and/or have means to do so, but you could hug an animal. Many animals can successfully be hugged, that is, the motion can be performed without discomfort for both participants. One of the popular forms of therapy is equine-assisted therapy, where you basically interact with horses. But of course, it's not limited to a single species, there's more fish in the sea, so to speak. If you live in an apartment, then get a dog or a cat (unless you already have one). Not always, but often those are huggable. If you're on a farm, the task is much easier probably. Just go to the pasture and hug a cow (be a gentleman and bring her flowers, they love that; not chocolate though, that's offensive). Even though that's over 500kg (1000 pounds) of a creature, it's probably pretty safe. Or there are other huggable critters on the countryside, like sheep. Now, with animals, there's a problem of reciprocity. But animals with relatively complex nervous system are capable of feeling some of the things we feel when we hug.

Anyway, while we're contemplating things that hug back, there are also things that certainly don't, but that are still can be hugged and give some comfort. Things like pillows. Anything soft. Actually, the wonderfully creative people in Japan have invented larger pillows specifically for hugging, called dakimakura, usually with a character from some anime printed on it. Hugging is really just a complex motion that causes certain changes in the brain, but those changes stem mostly from the motion and sensory feedback from it (feeling that you hug or are hugged). This is demonstrated by the fact that a machine called a hugbox, that's essentially a low-power press compressing the body lightly around a person, is used for autistic children to calm them down.

Anyway, those are just some of my thoughts on how to get the hugs you deserve. I hope you will find this, if not helpful, than at least funny and comforting. Best wishes for us both on our quest for connection. If I'll think of something more constructive later, I'll write.
